questions.question: What does 'git add' do, and what is the difference between 'git add .' and 'git add filename'?
questions.title: git add: Staging Changes
questions.direct_answer: 'git add' moves changes from the working directory to the staging area; 'git add .' stages all changed/new files in the current directory, while 'git add filename' stages only that specific file.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Git's staging model and deliberate commit crafting
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Always using 'git add .' without thinking — this can accidentally stage sensitive files like .env
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention 'git add -p' (patch mode) to stage specific hunks within a file

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: So 'git add' is the command that moves your changes from the working directory into Git's staging area — also called the index. Until you do this, Git is tracking that your files changed, but it won't include those changes in the next commit. 'git add filename' is the precise version — you're saying 'I want this specific file's changes in my next commit.' 'git add .' is the shortcut that stages everything — all modified files, all new untracked files — in the current directory and below. It's convenient but you have to be careful. If you have a .env file with secrets or some large binary file you didn't mean to track, 'git add .' will happily stage those too. A pro tip: use 'git add -p' — the patch flag — which lets you interactively choose which specific chunks or hunks of a file to stage. This is really powerful when you've made two unrelated changes in the same file and want to split them into separate commits.

sections.title: Key Points
content: 'git add' moves changes from working directory → staging area (index)
'git add filename' stages a specific file; 'git add .' stages all changes in current directory
Staged changes are what goes into the next 'git commit'
Be careful with 'git add .' — use .gitignore to exclude files you never want staged
'git add -p' stages changes interactively hunk-by-hunk within files

questions.question: What information does 'git status' show?
questions.title: Understanding git status
questions.direct_answer: 'git status' shows which files are staged for the next commit, which are modified but not staged, and which are untracked (new files Git doesn't know about yet).

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of how to check Git state before committing
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not running git status before committing and accidentally including unwanted changes
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention 'git status -s' for short format output, useful in CI scripts

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Running 'git status' gives you a snapshot of your repository's current state across all three of Git's areas. It shows you three categories of files. First, 'Changes to be committed' — these are files in the staging area, ready for your next git commit. Second, 'Changes not staged for commit' — these files are tracked by Git and you've modified them, but you haven't run git add yet. Third, 'Untracked files' — these are brand new files that Git has never seen before and isn't tracking. It also tells you which branch you're on and whether you're ahead or behind the remote. I think of 'git status' as a sanity check I run before every commit — it tells me exactly what's going to be committed and catches anything I might have forgotten to add or accidentally modified. It's a zero-risk command, purely informational, so you can run it as many times as you want.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Shows three sections: staged (ready to commit), modified (changed but not staged), untracked (new files)
Also shows current branch and sync status with remote (ahead/behind)
Purely informational — safe to run at any time
'git status -s' gives a compact one-line-per-file short format
Run it before every commit as a habit to verify what you're about to commit

questions.question: What makes a good Git commit message, and what are conventional commit conventions?
questions.title: Good Git Commit Messages
questions.direct_answer: A good commit message is concise, written in the imperative mood, and explains what the commit does; conventional commits add a type prefix like 'feat:', 'fix:', or 'docs:' for machine-readable changelogs.

interviewer_intent.testing: Professional habits and understanding of team collaboration
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing messages like 'fix', 'changes', or 'wip' — these are useless for future debugging
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the 50/72 rule and conventional commits spec used for automated changelog generation

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A good commit message is one that helps your future self and your teammates understand what happened and why — without having to dig into the code. The classic rule is: write the subject line in the imperative mood, as if completing the sentence 'If applied, this commit will...' So 'Add user authentication endpoint' rather than 'Added authentication' or 'authentication changes'. The subject should be under 50 characters. If you need more detail, skip a line and write a body, keeping lines under 72 characters. The 'why' matters more than the 'what' — the code diff already shows what changed. As teams scale, many adopt the Conventional Commits specification — you prefix your message with a type: 'feat: add JWT refresh token support', 'fix: resolve NPE in UserService', 'docs: update API readme'. The types are machine-readable, so tools can automatically generate changelogs, determine semantic version bumps, and trigger CI pipelines. Bad examples to avoid: 'fix', 'asdf', 'changes', 'wip' — these make git log useless.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Write in imperative mood: 'Add feature' not 'Added feature' or 'Adding feature'
Subject line: under 50 chars; body: wrap at 72 chars; blank line between subject and body
Explain the 'why', not just the 'what' — the diff shows what changed
Conventional Commits: 'feat:', 'fix:', 'docs:', 'chore:', 'refactor:' prefixes
Avoid: 'fix', 'wip', 'changes', 'misc' — these make history unsearchable

questions.question: What is the difference between 'git diff' and 'git diff --staged'?
questions.title: git diff vs git diff --staged
questions.direct_answer: 'git diff' shows changes in the working directory that are NOT yet staged; 'git diff --staged' shows changes that ARE staged and will go into the next commit.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Git workflow knowledge — checking your own work before committing
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Running git diff after git add and being confused that nothing shows — because staged changes need --staged
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention 'git diff HEAD' which shows all changes (both staged and unstaged) vs last commit

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: These two commands answer slightly different questions. 'git diff' with no arguments compares your working directory — the files on disk — against the staging area. So it shows you changes you've made that you haven't staged yet. If you've already run 'git add' on a file, that file won't appear in plain 'git diff' anymore. That's where 'git diff --staged' comes in — it compares the staging area against the last commit, showing you exactly what will be captured in your next 'git commit'. Think of it as a preview of your commit. I use both regularly: 'git diff' to see what I've changed but haven't decided to commit yet, and 'git diff --staged' right before committing as a final review — did I stage the right things? There's also 'git diff HEAD' which bypasses the staging distinction and just shows everything changed compared to the last commit, staged or not.

sections.title: Key Points
content: 'git diff': working directory vs staging area — shows unstaged changes
'git diff --staged' (or '--cached'): staging area vs last commit — shows what will be committed
After 'git add', a file disappears from 'git diff' and appears in 'git diff --staged'
'git diff HEAD': shows all changes vs last commit, regardless of staging
Use 'git diff --staged' as a pre-commit review habit

questions.question: What does 'git commit --amend' do, and when should you use it?
questions.title: Amending the Last Commit with git commit --amend
questions.direct_answer: 'git commit --amend' rewrites the most recent commit — you can fix the commit message or add forgotten staged changes — but only use it on commits that haven't been pushed to a shared remote.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of Git history editing and awareness of the golden rule around shared commits
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Amending a commit that has already been pushed to a shared branch — this rewrites history and breaks other developers' repos
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that --amend creates a brand-new commit object with a new SHA, which is why it's dangerous on shared branches

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: git commit --amend lets you modify the most recent commit. Two common use cases: first, you just committed and immediately noticed a typo in the commit message — you can run 'git commit --amend' and your editor opens so you can fix the message. Second, you committed but forgot to include one file — you 'git add' the forgotten file, then run 'git commit --amend --no-edit' to add it to the previous commit without changing the message. The important caveat is that --amend technically creates a completely new commit object with a different SHA hash. The old commit is discarded. This means if you've already pushed that commit to a shared remote and someone else has pulled it, amending it would cause a history divergence that breaks their repository. The golden rule: only amend commits that exist only on your local machine and haven't been pushed to a shared branch. Once something is pushed and shared, create a new commit to fix it instead.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Rewrites the most recent commit — can fix the message or add forgotten staged changes
'git commit --amend --no-edit' adds staged changes to last commit without changing the message
Under the hood: creates a new commit object with a new SHA; the old commit is discarded
NEVER amend commits already pushed to a shared/public branch — it rewrites history
Safe to amend local-only commits that no one else has pulled
